### Navigation message authentication (NMA)

- Used in Galileo (OSNMA) and QZSS (QZNMA)
- "*Cryptography meets positioning*": Cryptographic material is provided to verify the authenticity of navigation message
- Based on \acr{TESLA} algorithm (more details in @perrig2000efficient):
  - Authenticity checks are based on comparing a received tag with a tag computed by the receiver using the navigation message and a key.
  - **keys** are disclosed later, so the receiver must buffer the data until the key is received and verified.
  - Why it works? An attacker cannot compute the correct tag without knowing the key, and the key is not known until it is disclosed.


### NMA process flow

![](assets/figures/session_5__added_value_services/osnma_workflow.svg){fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
1. Receiver collects [**navigation messages**]{style="color: #4097cfff; "}, OSNMA data ([**tag**]{style="color: #4cbe61ff;"}, [**chain key**]{style="color: #f5a20aff;"}, and [**root key**]{style="color: #d4471fff;"}) and buffers them.
2. The [**root key**]{style="color: #d4471fff;"} is authenticated with the **public key**.
3. The [**chain key**]{style="color: #f5a20aff;"} is authenticated with the [**root key**]{style="color: #d4471fff;"} (or a previously **authenticated key**).
4. Compute the [**tag**]{style="color: #6442a5ff;"} from the [**navigation message**]{style="color: #4097cfff; "} and the [**chain key**]{style="color: #f5a20aff;"}.
5. Compare the computed [**tag**]{style="color: #6442a5ff;"} with the received [**tag**]{style="color: #4cbe61ff;"}.
:::

### Where is OSNMA in Galileo?

- OSNMA is broadcast in the Galileo E1B signal, in the I/NAV message, see Section 4.3 of the [Galileo SiS ICD](https://www.gsc-europa.eu/sites/default/files/sites/all/files/Galileo_OS_SIS_ICD_in_force.pdf).

![OSNMA bits in Galileo, source: [Galileo OSNMA ICD](https://www.gsc-europa.eu/sites/default/files/sites/all/files/Galileo-OSNMA-SIS-ICD_in_force.pdf)](assets/figures/session_5__added_value_services/galileo-osnma-bits.svg){fig-align="center"}

### NMA validation timing

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant S as GNSS satellite
    participant R as Receiver

    S->>R: Transmit navigation bits (NMA data)
    Note over R: Buffer the navigation bits<br/>and wait for the tag
    Note over S,R: 30 seconds later
    S->>R: Transmit the hashed tag for the navigation bits
    Note over R: Store the tag hash<br/>and wait for the key
    Note over S,R: 30 seconds later
    S->>R: Reveal the key
    R->>R: Validate the key, hash message and validate tag
```


### Other authentication approaches

- \acr{CHIMERA} (in \acr{GPS}, [@ISAGT100A]) uses navigation message and pilot-channel watermarks (*markers*) for ranging authentication.
  - **Slow markers**: Once the navigation message is authenticated, a key is derived and used to generate a pseudo-random sequence of markers that are added to the pilot channel.
  - **Fast markers**: Alternatively, an *out-of-band* channel can be used to transmit the markers, e.g., via a cellular network.

![GPS Chimera adds markers to the pilot channel in L1C](assets/figures/session_5__added_value_services/chimera-gps-prn-puncturing.svg){fig-align="center"}

- Galileo \acr{SAS} leverages OSNMA keys to encrypt the E6-C ranging signal.


:::{.notes}
- GPS CHIMERA:
  - When signal is not authenticated, the receiver will experience a small correlation loss, that can be anyway compensated because the integration time for pilot channel can be increased.
:::

### Message Authentication limitations

- Not robust against *meaconing* (replay) attacks, where an attacker receives authentic signals and rebroadcasts them with a delay.
    - Could be mitigated if the receiver has a trusted time source, but this is not always the case.
- Authentication is not encryption: navigation message is still readable by anyone
- Authentication does not guarantee the accuracy or safety of the position.
- Authenticated position fixes (e.g. \acr{TTFAF}) will be in general delayed due to the time needed to receive the authentication data
